steps.title: Use the radius as the height of triangle HSP

lines.text: A radius meets a tangent at $90^\circ$, so the radius from $P$ to $[SH]$ is perpendicular to $[SH]$. It is the height of $\triangle HSP$, with base $|SH| = 58$.
$BK$ and $AH$ are both perpendicular to the tangent $HK$, so $BTHK$ has four right angles. It is a rectangle.

steps.title: Use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle ATB

lines.text: $|\angle ATB| = 90^{\circ}$, so the hypotenuse is $[AB]$.
A radius cannot be negative.
$|CD| = \frac{1}{2}|AB|$ and $|OB|$ is a radius, which is half the diameter, so $|CD| = |OB|$.
$|OC|$ and $|OD|$ are also radii, so all three sides of $\triangle ODC$ are equal.
An equilateral triangle has all angles $60^\circ$, so $|\angle ODC| = 60^\circ$.
$CD \parallel AB$, so the alternate angles are equal.

steps.title: Find the angle at A in triangle AOD

lines.text: $|OA| = |OD|$ (radii), so $\triangle AOD$ is isosceles and its base angles are equal.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius (diameter) at the point of contact, so $|\angle ABE| = 90^\circ$.
In $\triangle ABE$ the angles add to $180^\circ$, and $|\angle BAE| = |\angle OAD| = 60^\circ$.

steps.title: Use the opposite sides of the parallelogram

lines.text: In $FBQT$, the side $[TQ]$ is parallel and equal to $[FB]$. $[FB]$ goes straight up 5 units, so $T$ is 5 units directly below $Q$.
Plot $T(-2, 2)$ and join $F$, $B$, $Q$ and $T$ to see the parallelogram.
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\alpha$ equals $|\angle SPQ|$.
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to $180^\circ$.
A parallelogram is a four-sided shape whose opposite sides are parallel and equal in length.
A square has opposite sides parallel and equal in length.
So every square is a parallelogram: the statement is True.

skill.title: Construction 21: Centroid of a triangle
skill.output: accurate construction with construction lines shown

lines.text: Set the compass to more than half of $|AB|$. Put the point on $A$ and draw an arc above and below the line $AB$.
Keep the same compass width. Put the point on $B$ and draw two arcs that cross the first two arcs.
Join the two crossing points with a straight line. It meets $[AB]$ at its midpoint. Label this point $D$.
A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Join $C$ to $D$.
Find the midpoint $E$ of $[BC]$ by measuring: $|BC| = 10$ cm, so $E$ is $5$ cm from $B$. (Or bisect $[BC]$ with arcs as before.)
Join $A$ to $E$.
The medians cross at the centroid. Label this point $O$.

candidates.final: D \text{ is the midpoint of } [AB] \text{ and } O \text{ is the centroid}

lines.text: The centroid is where the three medians meet. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Measure $|BC|=11.7$ cm and mark the midpoint at 5.85 cm from $B$. Call this midpoint $D$.
Measure $|AC|=11.1$ cm and mark the midpoint at 5.55 cm from $A$. Call it $E$.
Join $A$ to $D$ and $B$ to $E$. Two medians are enough, since all three pass through the same point.
The centroid $G$ is where $[AD]$ and $[BE]$ cross. The third median, from $C$ to the midpoint of $[AB]$, also passes through $G$.

candidates.final: \text{Centroid } G \text{ is where the medians cross}

lines.text: The centroid is the point where the three medians meet. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, so two medians are enough.
Set the compass to more than half of $|PQ|$. Draw an arc above and below $PQ$ from $P$, then the same arcs from $Q$.
Join the two points where the arcs cross. This line cuts $PQ$ at its midpoint $M_1$. (Or measure $|PQ|$ and mark half of it.)
Repeat the arcs from $Q$ and $R$ and join the crossing points. This cuts $QR$ at its midpoint $M_2$.

steps.title: Draw two medians and mark the centroid

lines.text: Draw the line from $R$ to $M_1$ and the line from $P$ to $M_2$.
These medians cross at $G$, the centroid. A third median from $Q$ to the midpoint of $PR$ would pass through $G$ too.
